\chapter{That, and Why}
\label{ch:pa-that-and-why}
\hlchaptermodality{40}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hand a whole sentence to a verb with ki, give an opinion, ask why, and answer it with because.}

The complementiser and the reason. ki and ki differ by one stroke -- sihari against bihari, that against what -- and the book has taught the second since chapter 2 and never the first, so sochna had nothing to think. kyon is the one member of the k- question family the chapter-3 mnemonic left out, which is why cause could be neither asked for nor given; kyunki is those two words joined, so the answer is built entirely from what this chapter already gave.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ki]{\pa{ਕਿ} (ki) — that}

\label{lesson:PA-C40-ki}



\begin{quote}
From the chapter behind you, the two words for \emph{but}. And from the naming lesson, the word for \textbf{what}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{par}, \emph{lekin} — then \textbf{\pa{ਕੀ}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ate} — from two chapters back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Look at these two very carefully, because they are not the same word:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਕੀ}} — \emph{kī} — \textbf{what}, with the long bihari
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} — \emph{ki} — \textbf{that}, with the short sihari
\end{itemize}

One stroke apart, and completely different jobs. You have had \textbf{\pa{ਕੀ}} since you first asked someone's name. \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} is new.

\textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}} put two sentences \textbf{side by side}. \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} does something different: it lets one sentence be \textbf{swallowed} by another, as the thing a verb is about.

\begin{quote}
\emph{(verb of thinking, knowing or saying)} \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} \emph{(whole sentence)}
\end{quote}

English does the same with \emph{that}, and like English, Punjabi often drops it in speech. Learn it in place first.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{kī} and \emph{ki} — long, then short. Say them until they separate.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ki}, then any sentence you own, after it.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} two sentences joined by \emph{ate}, then one swallowed by \emph{ki}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What separates \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} from \textbf{\pa{ਕੀ}}, in writing and in meaning? (One stroke — sihari against bihari; \emph{that} against \emph{what}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maiṁ sochdā hāṁ ki]{\pa{ਮੈਂ} \pa{ਸੋਚਦਾ} \pa{ਹਾਂ} \pa{ਕਿ} — I think that…}

\label{lesson:PA-C40-sochda-ki}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, the swallowing word. And from the lesson that gave you \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ}}, the word for \textbf{I} and the copula that follows it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ki}, and \emph{maiṁ … hāṁ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ate} joining two sentences — from two chapters back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ} \pa{ਸੋਚਦਾ} \pa{ਹਾਂ} \pa{ਕਿ} …} — \emph{maiṁ sochdā hāṁ ki …} — \textquotedblleft{}I think that …\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Three of the four pieces are old: \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਂ}}, the habitual ending you met with \emph{bolda}, and \textbf{\pa{ਹਾਂ}}. Only \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} is new, and it opens the space your opinion goes into.

\textbf{A woman says \pa{ਸੋਚਦੀ}} — \emph{sochdī} — with the feminine ending, exactly as with every habitual verb this book has taught. The sentence you use is the one that matches you.

Everything you can already say can now be said \textbf{as an opinion} rather than as a fact. That is a large change for one small word, and it is the difference between reporting the world and having a view about it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the frame, in the form that matches you, and finish it.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} a bare sentence, then the same one inside the frame.
  \item \emph{Build:} an opinion whose inside half is negative.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give an opinion about anything you can name. Which piece of the frame was new today? (Only \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ki]{\pa{ਕਿ} reaches the page}

\label{lesson:PA-C40-ki-write}



\begin{quote}
One chapter back you wrote \textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}}, standing alone. Write it once from memory.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one stroke is the whole lesson}
Uncover both and put them side by side:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} — the short \textbf{\pa{ਿ}} sihari, written \textbf{before} the letter
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਕੀ}} — the long \textbf{\pa{ੀ}} bihari, written \textbf{after} it
\end{itemize}

Same consonant. The vowel stroke sits on a different side, and that alone is the difference between \emph{that} and \emph{what}. Both signs have been yours for many chapters; what is new is that the pair now matters.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Copy \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} once with the model in view, then \textbf{\pa{ਕੀ}} beneath it. Check which side each stroke fell on before you go on.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write both. Which one is \emph{that}, and how does its stroke sit? (\textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} — the sihari, before the letter.)

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} written — from two chapters back
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kyoṁ]{\pa{ਕਿਉਂ} (kyoṁ) — why}

\label{lesson:PA-C40-kyon}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back you wrote \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}}. And from the wellbeing lesson, the question word that taught you the family they all belong to.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}}, and \emph{kivēṁ} — every question word opens with \textbf{\pa{ਕ}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{jāṁ} — from two chapters back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਕਿਉਂ}} — \emph{kyoṁ} — \textbf{why}
\end{quote}

The same \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} as every question word in the family. This one has been missing: the book named the family when it taught \emph{kivēṁ}, listed its members, and \textbf{\pa{ਕਿਉਂ}} was the one it left out — so a reader could ask several things and never \textbf{why}.

That is not a small omission. \emph{Why} is the question that asks for a reason, and the next lesson is the word that answers it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kyoṁ?} — flat, as a whole question.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{kivēṁ?} and \emph{kyoṁ?} — how, and why.
  \item \emph{Say it:} the family's shared opening \textbf{\pa{ਕ}}, then \emph{kyoṁ}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask \emph{why}. What do every question word in this family share, and where were you first told so? (The opening \textbf{\pa{ਕ}}; the \emph{kivēṁ} lesson.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kyoṁki]{\pa{ਕਿਉਂਕਿ} (kyoṁki) — because}

\label{lesson:PA-C40-kyunki}



\begin{quote}
The two words this chapter has already given you.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{kyoṁ}, and \emph{ki}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{nā … nā …} — from two chapters back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The answer is the question with the swallowing word stuck to the end of it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਕਿਉਂ}} (\emph{why}) + \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} (\emph{that}) = \textbf{\pa{ਕਿਉਂਕਿ}} — \textbf{because}
\end{quote}

Both halves are already yours from earlier in this chapter; the join is the only new thing. Punjabi answers \emph{why} by saying, in effect, \textquotedblleft{}why-that\textquotedblright{}, and the reason then follows as a whole sentence.

\begin{quote}
\emph{(what happened)} \textbf{\pa{ਕਿਉਂਕਿ}} \emph{(the reason)}
\end{quote}

Note the \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} at the end is the short sihari one — the \emph{that} you learned, not the \emph{what}. Reading the word slowly is its own revision of the pair.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kyoṁ} — then \emph{kyoṁki}. The question, then the answer's opening.
  \item \emph{Build:} any sentence, \emph{kyoṁki}, and a reason.
  \item \emph{Run through:} ask \emph{kyoṁ?} and answer yourself.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask why, then answer it. What two words is \textbf{\pa{ਕਿਉਂਕਿ}} built from, and which \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}} is on the end? (\textbf{\pa{ਕਿਉਂ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਕਿ}}; the short sihari \emph{that}.) Next chapter: \textbf{if}, and \textbf{when}.
\end{tcolorbox}
